comment_text.value: very cool. on the auto sleep- how does wake work for agents that listen on an outbound connection rather than inbound HTTP? Claude Code remote control and Telegram bots in polling mode both hold a connection out and wait for messages. Once the sandbox sleeps nobody's listening, so a message sent from my phone never reaches it. Do you keep a relay outside the sandbox that holds those connections and wakes it, or are those agents expected to stay awake (and burn awake hours)?

comment_text.value:
Hey guys,

If you've used Claude Tag, you know the potential of it for orchestration, a few months ago I built a version of it as a Claude Code plugin, that brings the concept as a local version of it, simply as a always-on task driven Claude Code agent. Our clis, our local memory, our filesystem, our tools, for you or your team.

It's how I manage and orchestrate several projects across different companies, and how I've been running always-on agents since. Set one up under 5m, it's just Claude Code so you can run with any subscription including 20$, it's fully customizable and it has got some magic focused on token efficiency using claude code native features:

1. Chat through Claude Code channels (Discord, Telegram, iMessage etc). Handle permission prompts in chat, recalls past conversations, keeps per-channel rules ("remember this for this channel"), has per-user allowlists for teams, and you manage the session from chat: !model, !effort, !clear, !compact, !stop, etc.

2. Routines that only wake Claude when needed. Each routine can run on its own model and effort, and a precheck script decides whether the model runs at all. Example: triage new GitHub issues hourly, with a gh CLI precheck that only wakes the model when there are new untriaged issues.

3. Heartbeat that only wakes Claude when there are pending stuff waiting, quiet ticks mean 0 tokens.

4. Spawn and orchestrate local Claude Code sessions with the model and effort you want and let it steer using cross-messaging. In chat each task has it's own thread and you can steer sessions per thread. You can also change !model and !effort on a thread session.

5. Take over the agent or any session on the CLI or the Claude app. (all of them start with remote-control)

6. A watchdog handles auto-restart, and context hygiene compacts long sessions and clears them when idle. All configurable.

Feel free to explore the repo for full list of features ;)

Contributions are welcome!

story_title.value: Hermitd, a Claude Code plugin like Claude Tag, but local

comment_text.value: I tried organising my personal life with openclaw and claudeclaw but didn't like it very much. I been coding for over 30 years so I figured I should build one myself. It would have taken me months but with claude code I was able to do it in a few weekends. It essentially keeps a local copy of messages from whatsup, telegram, Gmail ( mail and calenders) , creates a vector index so that its searchable. I can create schedules to periodically scan and make daily briefings, reminders etc. I made a plugin interface so it was easy to integrated home assistant, unifi network, remote ssh, allsky so far. The github readme has some demo gifs.

comment_text.value:
VPS is production. Linux dev box is my local big box. Macbook just lets me move about and do iOS development. Orca lets me run agents either on linux box or locally on the macbook depending on how I'm feeling, and Orca handles all the worktrees & sub-agents for me (via Opencode). Everything runs in a tailscale network, ssh connects all the things.

My github repos all have CONSTITUTION.md files that keep multi-agent dev grounded. Production runs trigger github actions that automatically check logs daily, file bug reports, etc. I launch Orca and literally just type "checking in" and the CONSTITUTION.md file governs the scanning of github issues and prioritization of which issues need to be addressed. Another process prioritizes and bundles them. When I type "checking in" the Orca worktree handles the launching of sub-agents that fix things. Occasionally I weigh in with an opinion or pick a recommendation. If I'm in the mood to pay attention I'll ask it to find another round of bugs and let's keep going. Often I just let it close after the first round. When I tell it "done?" it does a full regression and a production box review. Code auto-deploys to production twice/day. I don't regularly push to production manually.

On Fridays the CONSTITUTION.md kicks off a strategy and roadmap review when I type "checking in". As I have ideas I add them to the roadmap in one of the worktrees. Generally nothing happens until they're reviewed on Fridays together, unless I push one manually.. which happens.

Hermes runs on the production box. I have a few skills and quick commands that lets me check in on production runs and the status of things. It's read-only by design, basically my version of a dashboard. If I have a thought, idea, research link, or question it'll write to a github issue and we'll deal with it in the next check-in.

Orca lets me do all this remotely from an iPhone, and I talk to Hermes via Telegram. I generally don't INITIATE new work using either of these. I report issues/ideas and let the process do the things. But I can, and have.. I just tend not to. The whole thing churns, and so my inclination to "jump in and do a thing" is less than before. My inclination now is to toss things into the machine and let the machine work the schedule. I'm at a point where I could easily automate 80% of this and do my manual things 1x/2x week and I think progress would stay steady. I'll get there at some point, but I like the level of engagement I'm participating in now.

Occasionally I use Claude Code as a watchtower review of things, or do a wholesale code review, or do a review of logs. But deepseek is much better at building this machine -- I built something manually over time and through a ship of theseus process it got ugly. Deepseek reviewed the situation and wrote the CONSTITUTION.md and designed the processes independently. It favors deterministic scripts for process but launches them via LLM and monitors for exceptions; also, no memory system which also disqualifies Claude from being at the center of this. Memory plugins didn't work well because instructions start accumulating all through the chain of instruction files (AGENTS.md, memory, etc) and that gets very undeterministic very quickly. Instructions are written once, reviewed/audited intentionally.. it's best not to let LLMs learn and write their own dynamically (yet).

I've since used it as a template for other projects I've started -- they work the same. Currently building the GTM agent that will handle all SEO, marketing, keywording, etc for my projects -- it'll be a significantly autonomous Hermes agent. Don't really need Claude for any of this and my Deepseek bill is $50-100/mo.

story_title.value: Claude Cowork and chat are now one Claude

comment_text.value: Main difference is agentconnect’s team collaboration layer. 1. Public facing agents can answer support questions. But they cannot access resources shared with private agents. 2. DM between a team member and an agent can stay private. Other team members cannot see them. 3. Each agent can have its own slack or telegram bot. Multiple agents can also work together in the same channel or thread. In hermes, each profile has its own messaging gateway and bot setup. 4. Each agent can access different code repos. It can also respond directly to issues, pull requests, code reviews, and check results. Another difference is the agent framework. Agentconnect uses acp. This lets teams run native codex, claude code, and other compatible agents. Hermes uses its own framework and supports models from different providers. In my experience, native coding agents are often easier to use for engineering teams. They also tend to produce better coding results. However, they may use more tokens than hermes.

story_title.value: A sandbox is not a permission model for multiagent systems

hits.comment_text:
Main difference is agentconnect’s team collaboration layer.
1. Public facing agents can answer support questions. But they cannot access resources shared with private agents.
2. DM between a team member and an agent can stay private. Other team members cannot see them.
3. Each agent can have its own slack or telegram bot. Multiple agents can also work together in the same channel or thread. In hermes, each profile has its own messaging gateway and bot setup.
4. Each agent can access different code repos. It can also respond directly to issues, pull requests, code reviews, and check results.
Another difference is the agent framework. Agentconnect uses acp. This lets teams run native codex, claude code, and other compatible agents. Hermes uses its own framework and supports models from different providers.
In my experience, native coding agents are often easier to use for engineering teams. They also tend to produce better coding results. However, they may use more tokens than hermes.
